prompt: Ana removes `db` and starts a new container with the same `-v pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data`. Why is the `loans` row still there?

choices.text: Docker copied the old container's layer into the new one
choices.why: Layers are never copied between containers.

choices.text: PostgreSQL keeps a copy in the image
choices.why: The image is read-only and identical for every container.

choices.text: The volume outlived the container
choices.why: Right: the data lives in `pgdata`. The container is new; the volume is the same one.

choices.text: The name `db` points to the same data
choices.why: Names are labels on containers; lesson 7 reused one and lost the data.

prompt: `docker volume inspect pgdata` shows a `Mountpoint` under `/var/lib/docker/volumes/`. How should Ana read or change the files in it?

choices.text: Edit them there with `sudo`, it is just a folder
choices.why: It is Docker's directory; editing behind the daemon's back is how lesson 6 said things break.

choices.text: Copy the folder somewhere else first
choices.why: Reading Docker's directory directly is the problem, copied or not.

choices.text: Through `docker commit`
choices.why: Commit captures a container's writable layer, not a volume.

choices.text: Through a container that mounts the volume
choices.why: Right, as the backup did.

prompt: Ana's volume holds data written by PostgreSQL 16. She starts `postgres:17` against it. What should she expect?
hint: What does the volume hold, and in which format?

choices.text: It needs PostgreSQL's own upgrade procedure
choices.why: Right: the files' format changed between major versions. A volume keeps bytes; it cannot convert a database.

choices.text: The new version uses the old files as they are
choices.why: Within one major version that is true; across 16 and 17 the format changes.

choices.text: Docker converts the volume automatically when the version changes
choices.why: Docker knows nothing about what is inside a volume.

choices.text: The volume is copied into the new image
choices.why: Volumes never enter images.

prompt: In the backup command, what does `:ro` in `-v pgdata:/data:ro` guarantee?

choices.text: The archive will be read-only
choices.why: The archive was written to `/backup`, a different mount.

choices.text: The backup container cannot change the volume
choices.why: Right: the volume is mounted read-only for that container.

choices.text: The database is paused during the backup
choices.why: Nothing pauses PostgreSQL; that is why a running database needs `pg_dump`.

choices.text: Only root may read the volume afterwards
choices.why: `:ro` affects this mount, inside this container.

prompt: With `site` bind-mounted on `/srv`, Ana appends a line to `site/index.html` on the host. When does the running container see it?

choices.text: After `docker restart web`
choices.why: No restart was needed; the second `cat` showed it.

choices.text: Never; the container got a copy when it started
choices.why: A bind mount is the same directory, not a copy.

choices.text: Immediately
choices.why: Right. Both sides are looking at the same files.

choices.text: Once the container's next `docker commit` runs
choices.why: Commit is not involved; the mount shows host files directly.

prompt: A container wrote `report.txt` into Ana's bind-mounted directory, and `ls -l` shows it owned by `root`. Which option prevents that next time?
hint: Run the process as somebody else.

choices.text: `:ro` at the end of the mount
choices.why: Read-only would stop the write altogether.

choices.text: `--privileged`
choices.why: That gives the container more power, not a different owner.
`--rm` removes the container; the file stays root's.

choices.text: `--user "$(id -u):$(id -g)"`
choices.why: Right: the process runs with Ana's numbers, so its files are hers.

prompt: Bruno's Dockerfile installs the program's dependencies into `/app/vendor`. He runs the image with his source directory bind-mounted on `/app`, and the program says its dependencies are missing. Why?
hint: What happens to a directory the mount lands on?

choices.text: The mount is laid over `/app`, hiding what the image had there
choices.why: Right. Whatever the image put in `/app` is invisible while the mount is in place.

choices.text: The bind mount deleted `/app/vendor` from the image
choices.why: The image is untouched; a container without the mount still has it.

choices.text: Dependencies cannot be installed in a Dockerfile
choices.why: They can; the problem is what the mount does to them at run time.

choices.text: Bind mounts are read-only by default, so the program cannot open its files
choices.why: They are writable unless `:ro` is asked for.

prompt: A container writing into a mount that ends in `:ro` fails with the message "Read-only file ___".
hint: The last word of the error.

prompt: Why does the lesson write `-v "$PWD/site":/srv` instead of `-v site:/srv`?
hint: What would Docker take `site` to be?

choices.text: Quotes are compulsory around every path
choices.why: They protect spaces in `$PWD`; they are not the point.

choices.text: A bare name means a volume
choices.why: Right: a bind mount needs an absolute host path, and `site:/srv` would create a named volume called `site`.

choices.text: `site` is a reserved word in Docker
choices.why: It is not; it would simply become a volume name.

choices.text: Relative paths are slower
choices.why: Speed is not involved.

prompt: Match each need to the mount the lesson recommends.

pairs.left: Source code Ana edits while the container runs
Short-lived scratch files that must not reach the disk

right_distractors: The container's writable layer, committed every night

prompt: A script mounts `--mount type=bind,source=/data/inbox,target=/in`, and `/data/inbox` was mistyped. What does `--mount` do that `-v` would not?

choices.text: It creates the directory, owned by root
choices.why: That is what `-v` does, silently.

choices.text: It mounts an empty tmpfs instead
choices.why: It mounts nothing and reports the error.

choices.text: It refuses to start the container
choices.why: Right: "bind source path does not exist". A typo stops the run.

choices.text: It falls back to a named volume
choices.why: No fallback; the container does not start.

prompt: With `--tmpfs /scratch:size=16m`, how many bytes did `dd` manage to write before "No space left on device"?
Why do production setups lean on named volumes and development setups on bind mounts?
hint: Which one depends on the host's layout?

choices.text: Bind mounts are slower on servers
choices.why: Speed is not the argument the lesson makes.

choices.text: Named volumes are encrypted by Docker before writing
choices.why: Nothing about a local volume is encrypted by default.

choices.text: Bind mounts are deprecated outside development
choices.why: They are fully supported; they just tie a command to one machine's layout.

choices.text: It ties a command to one machine's paths
choices.why: Right: a named volume works wherever Docker runs, and in development that path is exactly the point.

prompt: Bruno archives `pgdata` with `tar` every night while PostgreSQL runs. What is wrong with that backup?
hint: What is PostgreSQL doing to those files meanwhile?

choices.text: Writes happen during the copy
choices.why: Right: the copy need not be a consistent database. Stop the container first, or use `pg_dump`.

choices.text: Nothing, `tar` copies files atomically
choices.why: It copies one file after another while they keep changing.

choices.text: The archive is owned by root
choices.why: True in the lesson, and fixable, but not what makes the backup unreliable.

choices.text: Volumes cannot be mounted twice
choices.why: They can; the backup container mounted it alongside the database.
